title: 7 ways to clarity
author: Melissa Muth Martinez
summary: Muth Martinez argues that workplace ambiguity is not harmless and that replacing it with clarity is a leader's responsibility and a moral imperative. Ambiguity erodes trust, burns people out as they decode what is unsaid, and hides behind appealing words like flexibility and empowerment, especially in mission-driven nonprofits and academia. Responding to a question from Roi Ezra, she offers seven practices that any team member or leader can use. These include leading with curiosity, asking for the right information, requesting examples, repeating back what was heard, getting things in writing, asking for feedback regularly and naming what is awkward. The piece is practical and speaks in scripts, though it rests on personal experience rather than evidence, and it ends with a paid-subscription pitch.
points: Ambiguity quietly erodes trust and energy, and it often passes itself off as flexibility or empowerment.
Clarity is framed as a form of leadership that protects people's energy.
Ask for the right information by naming which part of the what, why, when or how is unclear, rather than asking for more of it.
Repeating back what you heard and getting agendas and action items in writing are simple ways to remove misalignment.
Asking for feedback explicitly and often, and naming what feels awkward, builds the trust that makes clarity possible.
quotes: Ambiguity can seem harmless—but it’s not. It chips away at trust. People hesitate, second-guess, stall, overcompensate. They burn out trying to read between the lines—from all that emotional labor required to figure out what’s not being said.

In mission-driven spaces like nonprofits and academia, ambiguity can be especially rampant. Passion is high, but clarity is often low. Job descriptions are aspirational, but they’re not really practical. Expectations are there, but no one can really tell you where they’re written.

However, we know that ambiguity is sneaky—it hides behind itself. It masquerades as things that people want. Flexibility, freedom, empowerment. Again, it all sounds harmless, but what actually happens is the things that need to be said—the ones that that drive results—the ones that save time and energy—struggle to see the light of day. And the longer ambiguity lingers beneath the surface, the harder it is to name—let alone fix.
Clarity isn’t just about getting “more information”—it’s about getting the right information. Are we confused by the goal?

It has always been absolutely shocking to me when meetings don’t have clear agendas, notes, or action items, but when I began leading an ADA office, the benefits of clear meeting structures and takeaways became even more evident to me. It’s not just that written communication helps people cover their butts, but it gives folks something to lean into after the conversation’s over—while respecting different learning needs.

Ambiguity flourishes in environments absent of (or averse to) feedback. But when team members are comfortable enough to ask their leaders for feedback and leaders are humble enough to do the same, dialogue become richer and naturally, clarity grows.

Moving away from ambiguity and towards clarity is a moral imperative. And whether we’re a member of a team of a leader of a team, there’s a role to be played. Clarity is how we protect people’s energy. How we build trust. How we stop spinning our wheels and actually move forward on the journey.
